Adult WEBL provisioning behavior in heat

Questions & Hypotheses

  1. How do adult birds with active nests change their provisioning behavior during hot periods? We hypothesized that adult birds will
  1. (H1) reduce their provisioning rates during hot periods because they must put more time and/or energy into thermoregulation to avoid hyperthermia and
  2. (H2) maintain total provisioning visits by increasing visit rates during cooler hours of the day.
  1. How does female body condition mediates provisioning We hypothesized that females in better condition (mass/tarsus) would be
  1. (H1) less likely than females in worse condition to reduce their visits during hot periods because they are able to mobilize the energy required to engage in more energetically costly active thermoregulatory behaviors and
  2. (H2) more likely than females in worse condition to maintain total provisioning visits by increasing visit rates during cooler hours of the day.
  1. How does heat affect baseline and stress-induced? Elaborate Hp for baseline and stress-induced
  1. H1: females that experienced heat over the prior day will be more likely to show elevated baseline corticosterone levels because they may upregulate their HPA axis in response to more challenging heat conditions
  2. H2: females that experienced heat over the prior week will be more likely to show elevated stress-induced corticosterone levels because challenging environmental conditions are correlated with elevated stress-induced corticosterone levels.
  1. Are provisioning rates affected by circulating CORT levels? We hypothesized that
  1. (H1) females with elevated baseline corticosterone concentrations after a hot period would be more likely to maintain provisioning delivery to nestlings during following hot periods because they have the capacity to upregulate their HPA axis in response to environmental challenges (Mentesana and Hau 2022). Furthermore, we hypothesized that Look at this paper: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/1365-2656.12843
  2. Stress – induced levels? Please elaborate a Hp.
  1. Does body condition mediate cort response?
  1. (H1) females in better body condition would be more likely to show elevated baseline cort after a hot period because they have the energetic capacity to respond to stress
  2. (H2) Females in better body condition would be less likely to show elevated stress-induced corticosterone after a hot period than females in worse body condition.

           family = nbinom2(),
           ziformula = ~ attempt_id,
           data = dplyr::filter(p,!is.na(mean_temp),

Conclusion: use glmmTMB, negative binomial, with zero-inflation factor attempt_id (assuming that some pairs are just more likely to not feed than other pairs)

Question 1: How do adult birds with active nests change their provisioning behavior during hot periods?

Hypothesis 1: We hypothesized that adults will reduce their provisioning rates during hot periods because they must put more time and/or energy into thermoregulation to avoid hyperthermia

Prediction: negative correlation between temp and provisioning

So provisining decreases with temp in forest, increases with temp in orchard, and does not change in grassland or row crop. Overall, no changes. So land cover is mediating responses to temp. So this means that the land cover interaction model is the one I should be using for provisioning. The causal links are interesting though - if condition mediates provioning responses to heat and land cover drives condtion, then adding land cover to the condition model might open a backdoor path and obscure the causal relationship between condition and provisioning.

Another question out of this is, are the adults responding to their own physiological state or are they responding to nestlings’ condition? The tough part is that I could imagine that they’re responding to nestlings’ begging behavior. Does begging behavior peak at some intermediate condition (i.e. when nestlings are really hungry but not yet weakened by it), or is it strongest when nestlings are fed well?

From the reading, it looks like what we should expect is that in resource-poor environments (i.e. agriculture), provisioning should respond to quality of nestlings, whereas in resource-poor environments, provisioning should respond to need of nestlings. But also, in the short term, nestling begging rate is driven by hunger, and generally reduced in small nestlings in large broods.

Q1H2

How do adult birds with active nests change their provisioning behavior during hot periods? We hypothesized that adult birds will

  1. (H2) maintain total provisioning visits by increasing visit rates during cooler hours of the day. Because of the spottiness of the data, I don’t think I’ll be able to compare whole days to other whole days. Instead, I think what we should expect is that morning - afternoon average hourly visits will be greater when max daily temp is greater.

First step is to summarize the provisioning data over morning vs afternoon and subtract.


p_sum <- p %>% 
  mutate(temp_code = if_else(mean_temp < 30, "c","h")) %>%
  group_by(site,attempt,habitat,species,attempt_id,nestbox,julian_date,date,year,year_fct,temp_code,mean_nestling_age,mean_nestling_condition,female_condition,brood_size,cort_s1_mother,cort_s2_mother) %>%
  summarize(max_temp = max(mean_temp,na.rm = TRUE),
            mean_temp = mean(mean_temp, na.rm = TRUE),
            min_temp = min(mean_temp,na.rm = TRUE),
            mean_visits = mean(valid_detections,na.rm = TRUE),
            n = n(),
            .groups = "keep") %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = temp_code,values_from = c(max_temp, mean_temp, min_temp, mean_visits,n)) %>%
  mutate(diff_visits = mean_visits_c - mean_visits_h,
         diff_temp = mean_temp_h - mean_temp_c) %>%
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(diff_visits))

Now that I have the dataset, I can model it. Will use similar covariates to provisioning model. Wonder if I’ll need to use a zero inflated model this time? Because it’s a mean of counts, might be able to use a Gaussian model.

m_WEBL <- lmer(sqrt(diff_visits) ~ diff_temp_scaled + mean_nestling_age_scaled + brood_size_scaled + year_fct + (1|site:attempt_id),

                                    !is.na(year_fct),
                                    !is.na(site),
                                    !is.na(attempt_id),
                                    species == "WEBL") %>%
                 mutate(across(c(diff_temp,mean_nestling_age,brood_size),
                               ~ scale(.x)[,1],
                                                    .names = "{.col}_scaled"))
                                                    )

TRES respond to max temp by increasing their hot hours visits… huh

Q2H1

  1. How does female body condition mediates provisioning We hypothesized that females in better condition (mass/tarsus) would be
  1. (H1) less likely than females in worse condition to reduce their visits during hot periods because they are able to mobilize the energy required to engage in more energetically costly active thermoregulatory behaviors

This implies an interaction between condition and temperature. I’m going to drop the habitat term from Q1H1

WEBL

    ylim(-5,200) +
    geom_text(data = dat_text_tres_q2h1, mapping = aes(x = -Inf, y = Inf,label = label),hjust = -.2, vjust = 1.2,inherit.aes = FALSE) +

So for TRES, when females are in better body condition, there’s more provisioning, and when it’s hot, there’s also more provisioning. But no interaction between the two.

Q2H2

  1. How does female body condition mediates provisioning We hypothesized that females in better condition (mass/tarsus) would be
  1. (H1) less likely than females in worse condition to reduce their visits during hot periods because they are able to mobilize the energy required to engage in more energetically costly active thermoregulatory behaviors and
  2. (H2) more likely than females in worse condition to maintain total provisioning visits by increasing visit rates during cooler hours of the day.

Q3H1

  1. How does heat affect baseline and stress-induced? Elaborate Hp for baseline and stress-induced
  1. H1: females that experienced heat over the prior day will be more likely to show elevated baseline corticosterone levels because they may upregulate their HPA axis in response to more challenging heat conditions
  2. H2: females that experienced heat over the prior week will be more likely to show elevated stress-induced corticosterone levels because challenging environmental conditions are correlated with elevated stress-induced corticosterone levels.
